I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

The people responsible have faced no consequences
There is something wrong with me as a person

vignette:
Sameer sits rigidly in the chair, his medic’s uniform immaculate, a stark contrast to the chaos he describes. For months, the world has been closing in on him, a process so gradual he almost didn’t notice until the walls were touching his shoulders. It all began a year ago, but the memories feel as if they are happening now, not in the past. He remembers the specific heat of that evening, the way his ex-partner, David, had come home from the base gym. The sharp, animal smell of sweat had filled their small apartment, an odour that Sameer now finds unbearable. David had been wearing a grey, sleeveless t-shirt, the kind Sameer has since purged from his own wardrobe, unable to even look at the fabric. The argument that followed was a blur of motion and hot, searing pain, but certain fragments remain burned into his mind. He can still feel the phantom ache in his ribs where David’s knee had connected, a physical echo that returns with startling clarity whenever a memory breaks through. When he tries to speak about it, the words refuse to form; it’s a memory made of sensation and scent, not language.

In the aftermath of leaving David, Sameer believed he had escaped. He met and married a kind woman, transferred to a new post, and tried to rebuild. But the past followed him. The scent of body odour on a crowded bus can send a jolt of terror through him so potent he has to get off at the next stop, gasping for air. He stopped exercising entirely, unable to tolerate the feeling or smell of his own sweat, which felt like a betrayal by his own body. His once athletic frame has softened, another mark of the man he no longer is. The avoidance has bled into his work. As a military medic, he is surrounded by authority, but the sight of a commanding officer or a military police officer now triggers a silent, sickening panic. He sees David’s unassailable confidence in their posture, hears the same tone of command in their voice. He feels small, powerless, just as he did on the floor of his apartment.

His life has become a carefully curated set of safe zones. Home is manageable, but only certain rooms. Work is a minefield he navigates with clenched fists. He has withdrawn from friends, from his new wife’s family, and even from his own relatives who remind him of David’s, the people who knew and did nothing. He is certain they see the same weakness in him that he sees in himself. There is something fundamentally wrong with him, he has come to believe, a deep, structural defect for allowing it to happen. He is a soldier, a medic trained to handle the worst of human injury, yet he could not protect himself. This thought is a constant, corrosive presence. It has leached the meaning from everything he once valued. Saving lives feels pointless when his own feels so irrevocably broken. The injustice of it all is a bitter pill; David faced no consequences, his career flourishing while Sameer’s world crumbles.

At night, the threat feels most immediate. Sleep offers no refuge. He lies awake for hours, his body rigid, listening. Every creak of the floorboards, every car door slamming in the street, sends a shockwave through his system. He has to stay alert, certain that danger is just outside the door. Sometimes, a memory will ambush him in this state of exhausted vigilance. He won’t just remember; he will be back there, the rough texture of the carpet against his cheek, the smell of sweat overwhelming him, feeling as if it’s all happening again for the very first time. It was after one such night, when the sound of his wife dropping a spoon in the kitchen made him cry out and dive for cover, that he finally made this appointment. He came seeking help not with any real hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified that this is all his life will ever be: a man in a uniform, trapped in a room, waiting for a blow that has already landed.
